meta.title: Who really said "Times are bad. Children no longer obey their parents, and everyone is writing a book"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Cicero. No work of his contains it. Quote Investigator traces the saying to a 1908 "ancient tablet" story; the Cicero credit is documented only from 2001.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Times are bad. Children no longer obey their parents, and everyone is writing a book'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Cicero. Quote Investigator traces this to an "ancient tablet" story first printed in 1908; the Cicero version is documented only from a 2001 magazine filler.

answer.label: Not Cicero — an anonymous saying with no ancient source
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · ancestor text first printed August 1908
answer.sourceLine: No work of Cicero is ever named as the source, and neither Quote Investigator ↗ nor Wikiquote ↗ traces it to one — Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed.” It is the last stop on a wandering “ancient tablet” story: a lament about corrupt politics, disrespectful children and everyone wanting to write a book, printed in August 1908 as a translation of an inscription in the Imperial Museum at Constantinople, then re-dated and re-assigned for decades to a Chaldean king, an Assyrian tablet and an Egyptian priest before turning up as Cicero’s. QI finds no compelling evidence any such tablet inscription exists.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: None — no speech, letter or treatise is ever named
Bassett’s Scrap Book, vol. 6, no. 6 (August 1908), p. 84
InfoWorld, 16 April 2001, p. 49 — as cited by Quote Investigator and Wikiquote
Apocryphal — no evidence of an ancient tablet, no Cicero

source.excerpt: The “good old times” seemed as bad to the “good-old-timers” as the present times seem to the modern man, as shown by the following translation of an inscription on a tablet in the Imperial Museum at Constantinople, Turkey:— Naram Sin, 5000 B. C. We have fallen upon evil times, the world has waxed old and wicked. Politics are very corrupt. Children are no longer respectful to their elders. Each man wants to make himself conspicuous and write a book.
trail: August 1908 — a cycling magazine. The oldest known printing is not ancient at all: a filler item in Bassett’s Scrap Book, the official organ of the League of American Wheelmen, offering “the following translation of an inscription on a tablet in the Imperial Museum at Constantinople” and dating it to Naram Sin, 5000 B.C. The page is readable in the Internet Archive scan ↗.

1913–1948 — the tablet keeps moving. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ tracks the date sliding from 5000 B.C. to 3800 B.C. (Iowa philosophy professor George T. W. Patrick, Popular Science Monthly, May 1913) to 2800 B.C. (Connecticut State Librarian George S. Godard, 1922), the material changing from stone to papyrus (Bennett Cerf, 1948), and the speaker changing from Chaldean king to Assyrian scribe to Egyptian priest.

2001 — Cicero’s name gets attached. By 2001 the saying had been boiled down to one sentence and credited to “Marcus Tullius Cicero, statesman, orator, and writer (106–43 B.C.)” in InfoWorld of 16 April 2001, p. 49 — the citation carried by both Quote Investigator and Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗.

The Library of Congress got there first. Respectfully Quoted, entry 456 ↗ files the saying under “Tablet, Babylon,” records the 1949 and 1953 printings behind it, and concludes that both “would seem to be spurious” — suggesting the book-writing line may simply echo Ecclesiastes 12:12.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest known printing of the saying, not the Cicero wording. The familiar one-sentence version — “Times are bad. Children no longer obey their parents, and everyone is writing a book” — is a much later condensation; Quote Investigator records it attached to Cicero’s name by 2001.

source.rightsNote: No status is asserted. The exact circulating wording has no identified author or first publication — it is an anonymous condensation of a saying that has been rewritten repeatedly since 1908, so there is nothing to date a copyright term from. The 1908 Bassett’s Scrap Book ancestor text quoted above is itself long out of copyright in the United States, but that does not extend to the modern one-sentence version.

author.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.kicker: The man it gets pinned on
author.heading: Who Cicero actually was
author.metaLine: 106–43 BC · Roman statesman, orator and philosopher
author.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero (born 3 January 106 BC, killed 7 December 43 BC) was a Roman statesman, lawyer, orator and philosopher who reached the consulship in 63 BC and spent that year suppressing the Catilinarian conspiracy. Because so much of his writing survives, and because he really did specialise in O tempora, o mores!, he is one of the internet’s favourite places to park an unsourced grumble about civilisational decline. This is one of those: a modern one-liner with no Latin behind it, no manuscript, and no Cicero.

Attribution history traced in Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: Ancient Tablet: The World is Speedily Coming to an End. Everyone Wants to Write a Book,” October 22, 2012, which records the condensed Cicero-credited wording in InfoWorld, April 16, 2001, 49. Listed as misattributed to Cicero in Wikiquote, “Cicero.”

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been credited with this
misattribution.intro: Almost nothing about this quotation is stable. Over roughly a century the words changed, the date moved by thousands of years, the tablet became papyrus, and the speaker was reassigned several times — Cicero being only the most recent tenant.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists it under “Misattributed,” sourcing it no further back than InfoWorld, 16 April 2001, p. 49. No speech, letter or treatise of Cicero’s is ever named, and Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ shows the wording arriving from an early-1900s newspaper-and-magazine story, not from antiquity.

items.who: “Naram Sin, 5000 B.C.” — an unnamed tablet in Constantinople
items.why: This is the form in the August 1908 Bassett’s Scrap Book item, which names no king and no kingdom — only “Naram Sin” and a date, above a translation of an inscription said to be in the Imperial Museum at Constantinople, readable in the Internet Archive scan ↗. By May 1913 the philosopher George T. W. Patrick was telling it as “King Naram Sin of Chaldea, 3800 years B.C.,” and by 1922 the date had moved again, to 2800 B.C.

items.who: An Assyrian clay tablet of about 2800 B.C., held in Constantinople
items.why: The best-travelled version, printed in a 1922 report by the State Librarian of Connecticut and repeated for decades after. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes there is “no compelling evidence” that any of these wordings was inscribed on an Assyrian tablet.

A 1925 Big Brother and Big Sister Federation publication reassigned the lament to “an Egyptian 6,000 years ago,” and a 1948 note in the journal World Affairs gave it to an Egyptian priest — both documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No ancient tablet has ever been produced, and no Cicero: Quote Investigator finds no compelling evidence that any of these wordings was inscribed in antiquity. The oldest known text is a filler paragraph in an American cycling magazine of August 1908, and the Library of Congress’s own reference work had already concluded that the printings behind the tablet story “would seem to be spurious” in Respectfully Quoted, entry 456 ↗.

context.heading: Why this one keeps working
lead: The quotation is a joke with a delivery mechanism attached. The punchline — that people have always thought the world was going to the dogs, and that the last straw is everybody writing a book — only lands if the words are genuinely ancient. So the story has always needed a source, and for more than a century it has borrowed whichever one sounded most impressive: a Chaldean king, an Assyrian tablet, an Egyptian priest, an ancient scrap of papyrus, and finally Rome’s most quotable orator.

Cicero is an unusually comfortable host for it, because he really did make a career of exactly this complaint. O tempora, o mores! — “Oh the times! Oh the customs!” — appears in four of his surviving speeches, most famously at the opening of the First Catilinarian, delivered in 63 BC. The trouble is that the sentence circulating under his name is not a translation of anything he wrote; it is a modern compression of an English paragraph that first appeared in print in 1908.
context.detailsSummary: How a 1908 magazine filler became a Roman epigram
detailsBody: Each retelling trimmed something. The 1908 version has four complaints: evil times, corrupt politics, disrespectful children, and self-promoting authors. By 1922 an apocalypse had been added and the date had dropped from 5000 B.C. to 2800 B.C. By 1948 the tablet had become papyrus and the whole thing had shrunk to two clauses. The version now circulating keeps only the two clauses that still get a laugh — disobedient children and too many books — and prefixes them with a flat “Times are bad.”

The Library of Congress’s Respectfully Quoted offers a quieter possibility for the book-writing line: it may be an echo of Ecclesiastes 12:12, “of making many books there is no end” — a genuinely ancient complaint, just not the one being quoted.
context.pull: The saying is old enough to sound interesting and modern enough to be checkable — and the check keeps coming back the same way.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest known instance is the August 1908 Bassett's Scrap Book item (vol. 6, no. 6, p. 84) presenting it as a translation of a tablet inscription in the Imperial Museum at Constantinople dated 'Naram Sin, 5000 B.C.'; the article then tracks versions in 1913 (Patrick, Popular Science Monthly, 3800 B.C.), 1920, 1922 (Godard, Assyrian, 2800 B.C.), 1925 (Egyptian), 1936, 1938, 1948 (Bennett Cerf, papyrus) and 1948 (Egyptian priest, c. 4000 B.C.); states 'By 2001 a condensed version of the saying was being attributed to the famous Roman orator Cicero' citing InfoWorld, April 16, 2001, p. 49; and concludes there is 'no compelling evidence' that any of the quotations was inscribed on an ancient Assyrian tablet.

Wikiquote's Cicero article carries 'Times are bad. Children no longer obey their parents, and everyone is writing a book.' under the section heading 'Misattributed', sourced only to InfoWorld, Vol. 23, No. 16, 16 April 2001, p. 49, with a note that it had been attributed previously to many other sources from 1908 on per Quote Investigator.

Respectfully Quoted: A Dictionary of Quotations (Library of Congress, 1989), number 456, author 'Tablet, Babylon', gives 'The world must be coming to an end. Children no longer obey their parents and every man wants to write a book,' attributed to a tablet unearthed near Babylon dated 2800 B.C. (Leewin B. Williams, 1949), plus an expanded Assyrian-tablet version (Patty and Johnson, 1953), and states: 'Both of the above quotations would seem to be spurious. Perhaps "every man wants to write a book" may be related to "of making many books there is no end," Ecclesiastes 12:12.'

The full-text scan of Bassett's Scrap Book (vols. 5-6) contains, on the page headed '84 BASSETTS SCRAP BOOK', the passage: 'The "good old times" seemed as bad to the "good-old-timers" as the present times seem to the modern man, as shown by the following translation of an inscription on a tablet in the Imperial Museum at Constantinople, Turkey:— Naram Sin, 5000 B. C. We have fallen upon evil times, the world has waxed old and wicked. Politics are very corrupt. Children are no longer respectful to their elders. Each man wants to make himself conspicuous and write a book.'

The phrase 'O tempora, o mores!' appears in four extant speeches of Cicero — In Verrem 2.4.56, In Catilinam 1.2, De Domo Sua 137 and Pro Rege Deiotaro 31 — most famously in the opening of the First Oration against Catiline, delivered in 63 BC.

Marcus Tullius Cicero was born 3 January 106 BC and died 7 December 43 BC; he was a Roman statesman, lawyer, scholar, philosopher, orator and writer; he held the consulship in 63 BC, the year of the Catilinarian conspiracy.
